implementation_notes: The with statement is the language's bracket: __enter__ runs first, the block is the body, and __exit__ runs on every exit path. @contextlib.contextmanager lets one generator define both halves - everything before the yield is setup, the yield is where the body executes, and the code after it (usually in try/finally) is teardown - which is the direct replacement for the Smalltalk wrapper method. Use the decorator for the common case; state explicitly that the generator must not swallow exceptions (returning a true value suppresses them, which is almost never wanted), and note that since 3.2 the same object can also be used as a function decorator.
pitfalls: Forgetting to re-raise in the except branch makes the context manager swallow the body's exception, because a generator context manager treats a completed generator as handled.
A generator-based manager is one-shot: reusing the same instance (even as a decorator on two calls) raises RuntimeError, and reentrancy requires a class-based manager.
An exception raised while unwinding after the yield replaces the body's exception unless it is chained or suppressed deliberately.

variants.name: class implementing __enter__ / __exit__ (with ExitStack for dynamic sets)
variants.idiom_name: with Transaction() as conn: ... using __enter__/__exit__, plus contextlib.ExitStack
variants.implementation_notes: When the manager carries state, must be reusable or reentrant, or is the resource object itself, implement the protocol directly: __enter__ performs setup and returns the value bound by as, __exit__ receives the exception triple and returns whether to suppress it. contextlib.ExitStack composes a dynamic set of managers and callbacks inside one with statement (and AsyncExitStack does the same for async managers), which is the tool for resource sets whose size is only known at runtime. What replaces the classic wrapper is the protocol plus these stdlib containers; the generator form is shorter but one-shot, so the class is the right shape for anything reused.
pitfalls: __exit__ must not return a truthy value unless suppression is intended; returning True silently hides the body's exception and the program continues in an inconsistent state.

Managers that store state are not reentrant: reusing one instance across nested or repeated with statements re-runs setup on the same object - ExitStack documents this trap explicitly and recommends one stack per with statement.
An exception raised in __exit__ replaces the body's exception unless it is explicitly chained (raise ... from) or suppressed.
